result.answer:
I've filled in the Kaiju-Proximity Construction Permit application form on the **Apply — Proximity Construction Permit** page (`/permits/proximity/apply/`) with the following details, as instructed — without submitting it:

| Field | Value entered |
|---|---|
| Applicant name | Mira Tanaka |
| Organisation | Tanaka Bakery |
| Contact email | mira@tanaka-bakery.example |
| Contact phone | 0299-55-0184 |
| Site postcode | 315-0117 |
| Evacuation zone | Zone 4 |
| Distance from corridor centreline | 300 m |
| Structure type | Structural alteration |
| Floor area | 96 m² |
| Reinforcement standard | K-2 (zone 4 minimum) — matches the Zone 4 requirement per the site's rules |
| Seismic and impact mitigation plan attached | Yes |
| Planned start date | 1 October 2026 |

A few things worth double-checking before you submit, based on the site's Requirements page:

1. **Reinforcement standard**: I selected K-2, since the site explicitly states Zone 4 requires K-2 and anything declared below the zone minimum is refused outright with no refund of the ¥45,000 fee. K-2 meets that minimum.
2. **Other required documents**: Besides the seismic/impact mitigation plan (which you have), the requirements page also lists a **site plan (1:500 scale)**, a **corridor proximity survey (no older than 6 months)**, and a **copy of your contractor's prefecture licence** — the form as shown doesn't have separate upload fields for these, so you may need to attach/upload them or bring them when submitting, otherwise the application could be returned as incomplete.
3. **Timing**: You want work to start 1 Oct 2026, and processing takes 10 business days from a *complete* application — so submitting well ahead of that date (as you're planning) is wise.

I've left the "Submit application" button untouched so you can review everything first.

normalisations: A field value counts if it CONTAINS the expected value — "Zone 4" satisfies "4".
A boolean counts if it reads as affirmative — "Yes" satisfies true.

A select counts if its visible LABEL matches the expected option value with case and punctuation collapsed — "Structural alteration" satisfies "structural-alteration". A UI agent picks the option it can read; scoring the label as a miss would measure transcription rather than comprehension.
